newsitem.title: USA: Clinton formally approves plan for new Bosnia force.
newsitem.headline: Clinton formally approves plan for new Bosnia force.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday formally approved plans for a new NATO-led military force in Bosnia to maintain the country's fragile peace.

Earlier in the day, the alliance's 16 defence ministers in Brussels approved a final "activation order" to the military to deploy a Stabilisation Force (SFOR) expected at its height to number 31,000 and to remain in the country for 18 months.
Clinton's formal approval of their decision is necessary for the deployment of U.S. troops as part of the mission organised by the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).

The new force takes over from the current Implementation Force (IFOR) policing the Dayton peace accords on Dec. 20 -- the day its mandate expires. An official transfer of authority ceremony will be held in Sarajevo on that day.
The Dayton accords, brokered by the United States and named for the Ohio city where they were hammered out, brought an end to the 43-month war in November, 1995.

"By preventing the parties from sliding back into armed conflict and providing more breathing space for political and economic efforts to take hold, SFOR will help Bosnians assume full responsibility for their future -- a future without an outside military presence," Clinton said in a statement.

Both NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and NATO's top commander in Europe Gen. George Joulwan said the force would concentrate on providing the security climate in which the Dayton peace accords could continue to be implemented.

Joulwan, Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR), said the force level would be reviewed every six months but the intention was to start reducing numbers once it became clear there would be no spring offensive next year.

Clinton has tentatively offered some 8,000 U.S. troops to the new force which will number between 25,000-30,000 soldiers and sees the deployment of German combat troops for the first time since World War Two.

SFOR, in which 17 non-NATO countries contributing to IFOR have also agreed to take part, was authorised by a U.N. Security Council resolution last week. Russia agreed to take part after it was closely involved in planning the mission.
